passages.happening:
In the days of Jehoiakim, God tells Jeremiah to go to the Rechabite family, bring them into one of the chambers of the LORD's house, and give them wine to drink (verse 2). Jeremiah brings Jaazaniah and his brothers and all his sons, the whole Rechabite household (verse 3), into the room of the sons of Hanan, a man of God (verse 4). He sets out pitchers full of wine and cups and tells them to drink (verse 5).

They refuse. Their forefather Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them never to drink wine, they or their sons (verse 6), never to build a house, sow seed or plant a vineyard, but to live in tents all their days, so that they might live long in the land where they were strangers (verse 7). They have obeyed him in everything (verses 8 to 10).

They are in Jerusalem only because Nebuchadnezzar came into the land, and they fled to the city to escape the Chaldean and Aramean armies (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Verse 11 explains why these tent-dwellers were in a city. It fits the last years of Jehoiakim, around 599 to 598 BC, when after his rebellion raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites and Ammonites were sent against Judah.

Their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab appears in 2 Kings 10 as an ally of Jehu, who seized the northern throne around 841 BC and violently purged Baal worship. The family's rule was about two and a half centuries old by Jeremiah's day.

Living in tents, refusing to farm or drink wine, kept them apart from the settled life of Canaan and its gods. They kept their ancestor's command for generations, even in a city full of wine.
passages.later: Kings tells how Jehonadab son of Rechab joined Jehu, who asked him, ‘Is your heart as true to mine as my heart is to yours?’ (2 Kings 10:15). A psalm counts wine among God's gifts, ‘wine that gladdens the heart of man’ (Psalm 104:15).
passages.asks: The Rechabites kept a human ancestor's command for two hundred and fifty years. Ask what commitments you have kept that long, and to whom. And ask what in the surrounding culture you need to say no to, even when it is set in front of you.

passages.t: A family that kept its word, and a people that did not
passages.happening:
God tells Jeremiah to ask Judah and Jerusalem whether they will not learn a lesson and listen to his words (verse 13). ‘The words of Jonadab son of Rechab have been carried out’ (verse 14). His sons have obeyed their forefather to this day. But God has spoken to his people again and again, and they have not listened (verse 14). He sent his prophets to call them to turn from their evil ways and not follow other gods, and they did not listen (verse 15). The Rechabites obeyed their father's command, but these people have not obeyed God (verse 16). So God will bring on Judah every disaster he announced (verse 17).

Then Jeremiah tells the Rechabites that because they obeyed their forefather, God says Jonadab son of Rechab ‘will never fail to have a man to stand before Me’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The lesson is a contrast. A human family kept a human word for centuries. God's people would not keep the word of God, though he sent prophet after prophet.

God does not tell Judah to live like the Rechabites. He commends the Rechabites for their faithfulness to the rule they had received. Scripture elsewhere treats wine both as God's good gift and as dangerous when abused. Christians differ on whether abstaining is wise, and this passage does not settle that question.

To stand before God was the language of service, as priests and prophets stood before him. The promise to the Rechabites is that their family will always have someone in God's service.
passages.later: Jesus rebuked those who ‘disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men’ (Mark 7:8). Proverbs warns that wine misused ‘is a mocker’ (Proverbs 20:1).
passages.hard:
Is God endorsing abstinence from wine, or saying that every family tradition should be kept?

No on both counts, if the chapter is read on its own terms. God does not command Judah to live like the Rechabites; he commends the Rechabites for their faithfulness. Scripture treats wine both as a good gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15) and as dangerous when abused (Proverbs 20:1). Christians have differed on whether abstinence is wise, and this passage does not settle it. Nor is the lesson that every inherited custom must be kept; some traditions ought to be given up, and Jesus rebuked people who set aside God's command for the sake of their tradition (Mark 7:8-9).

The chapter turns on a contrast: a family kept a human word, and God's people would not keep God's.
passages.asks: God held up an obedient family as a rebuke to his own people. Ask whose faithfulness puts your own to shame. And ask what word of God you have heard again and again and not yet obeyed.
